lesson.title: A Date Which Will Live in Infamy: The Attack on Pearl Harbor
lesson.summary: On December 7, 1941, Japan launched a surprise attack on the United States Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, instantly ending American neutrality and bringing the United States fully into World War Two.
lesson.body:
Tensions with Japan had been building for years, separate from the war already underway in Europe. Japan's expansion into China through the 1930s, followed by its move into French Indochina after France's surrender in 1940, alarmed American policymakers. The United States, along with Britain and the Dutch, responded with economic pressure, including a 1941 embargo on oil and scrap metal exports to Japan that cut off resources its military badly needed. Even as Neutrality Act restrictions and isolationist opinion still pushed toward staying out of the war in Europe, this standoff with Japan was building toward a crisis of its own in the Pacific.

The United States had held the Philippines as a territory since acquiring it from Spain in 1898, giving it a direct military and strategic stake in East Asia that Japan's expansion now threatened. American bases scattered across the Pacific, including in the Philippines and at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, existed largely because of this long standing American presence in the region.

Early on the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese carrier based aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor without any declaration of war, sinking or damaging numerous battleships, including the USS Arizona, whose destruction killed more than 1,100 crew members, and killing over 2,300 Americans in total. Japanese forces launched coordinated attacks against American and other Allied positions across the Pacific that same day, including the Philippines.

Roosevelt addressed Congress the next day, December 8, 1941, calling it a date which will live in infamy and asking for a declaration of war against Japan, which Congress approved almost unanimously. On December 11, 1941, Germany and Italy, honoring their alliance with Japan, declared war on the United States, and the United States responded in kind. Years of official neutrality ended at once, and the United States found itself fighting in both the European and Pacific theaters of World War Two.
